title: The Empty Chair at Dinner Can Preach a Sermon About Eternity No Comfortable Sunday Ever Could
paragraphs: The Empty Chair at Dinner Can Preach a Sermon About Eternity No Comfortable Sunday Ever Could

There are moments when grief tears through every comfortable answer we have ever given about death—and in that unbearable silence, the resurrection of Jesus Christ becomes either everything or nothing.
There is an empty chair at the table.
Nobody moved it.
Maybe nobody has had the courage.

It still sits where it always sat, almost as though the person who belonged there might walk through the door again, apologize for being late, pull it backward across the floor, and sit down like nothing happened.
But something happened.
And everyone at the table knows it.
Maybe it was your father’s chair.
Your mother’s.
Your husband’s.
Your wife’s.
Your brother’s.
Your sister’s.
Your child’s.
Your best friend’s.
Maybe the loss happened years ago, and you thought you were finally learning how to carry it.
Then somebody cooked their favorite meal.
A familiar song started playing.
You found an old photograph while looking for something completely unrelated.
Someone laughed exactly the way they used to laugh.
Or you walked into the dining room and looked at that chair.
And suddenly...
you were back at the funeral.
That is one of grief’s cruelties.
It does not always knock before entering.
You can survive anniversaries you thought would destroy you, then fall apart on an ordinary Tuesday because you found their coffee cup behind another mug in the cabinet.
You can worship on Sunday and cry in the grocery store on Monday because you reached automatically for something they loved.
You can sincerely believe in Jesus Christ and still have nights when you would give almost anything just to hear that voice one more time.
And Christianity does not require you to pretend otherwise.
We sometimes speak about death so gently that we almost make the Bible sound embarrassed by grief.
We say, “They’re in a better place.”
We say, “Everything happens for a reason.”
We say, “Be strong.”
Sometimes those words are offered with genuine love.
But there are moments when the grieving heart does not need a slogan.
It needs something stronger than sentiment.
Because death is not sentimental.
Death separates.
Death interrupts.
Death leaves clothes hanging in closets and unfinished conversations trapped inside living hearts.
Death can turn a telephone number you once called without thinking into something you cannot bring yourself to delete.
Death can leave one side of a bed untouched.
Death can leave a birthday on the calendar belonging to someone who will not grow another year older in this present age.
And Scripture does something astonishing.
It does not ask us to call death beautiful.
Paul calls death an enemy.
That matters.
Christian hope is not built upon pretending death does not hurt.
Christian hope begins by looking death directly in the face...
and then looking beyond death to a risen Jesus Christ.
Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 15:20:
“But now Christ has been raised from the dead...”
Those opening words are thunder.
Νυνὶ δὲ — Nyni de — “But now.”
Everything changes there.

Paul has spent the surrounding argument explaining how catastrophic it would be if Christ had not risen. If there is no resurrection, Christian proclamation collapses. Faith becomes futile. Sin retains its verdict. Those who have died in Christ are lost.
Then comes the earthquake:
But now.
Christ has been raised.
Not merely remembered.
Not merely admired.
Not merely preserved through the teachings of His followers.
Raised.
The Greek expression Χριστὸς ἐγήγερται — Christos egēgertai declares that Christ has been raised from among the dead.
Christianity does not ultimately offer grieving people a philosophy about death.
It announces an event.
Jesus Christ was crucified.
Jesus Christ died.
Jesus Christ was buried.
And Jesus Christ rose.
That distinction is everything when you are staring at an empty chair.
Because if Jesus merely taught beautiful ideas and then remained inside Joseph’s tomb, grief eventually gets the final word.
If Jesus remained dead, every cemetery is telling us the ultimate truth about humanity.
If Jesus remained dead, the empty chair wins.
The coffin wins.
The grave wins.
Death wins.
But Paul refuses to leave us there.
“Νυνὶ δὲ Χριστὸς ἐγήγερται ἐκ νεκρῶν, ἀπαρχὴ τῶν κεκοιμημένων.”
Christ has been raised from the dead, “ἀπαρχὴ — aparchē”, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep.
Firstfruits.
That word carries enormous hope.
In the biblical world, the firstfruits were not merely an isolated piece of produce. They belonged to the beginning of a harvest.
Paul is saying something breathtaking.
The resurrection of Jesus is not merely an extraordinary miracle that happened to one Man long ago.
For those who belong to Christ, His resurrection is the beginning of the harvest.
The empty tomb is a promise that the cemetery does not receive the final chapter.
Paul continues:
“ὥσπερ γὰρ ἐν τῷ Ἀδὰμ πάντες ἀποθνῄσκουσιν, οὕτως καὶ ἐν τῷ Χριστῷ πάντες ζῳοποιηθήσονται.”
As in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive.
Notice how brutally honest Scripture is.
In Adam all die.
The Bible does not hide the human catastrophe.
Death entered the human story through sin. Humanity is not merely suffering from unfortunate biological inconvenience. Something has gone profoundly wrong between creation and Creator.
And eventually every empty chair points toward the same terrifying reality.
We are mortal.
You are going to die.
I am going to die.
The people we love will die unless Christ returns first.
Money cannot negotiate with the grave.
Beauty cannot charm it.
Success cannot outrun it.
Followers cannot cancel it.
Possessions cannot bribe it.
There will eventually be a final meal, a final conversation, a final photograph, a final heartbeat.
Most of us simply do not know when.
And perhaps that is why an empty chair can preach a sermon no comfortable Sunday ever could.
Because that chair asks questions we spend much of our lives avoiding.
What happens when my chair is empty?
What happens when people are talking about me in the past tense?
What happens when my possessions belong to somebody else?
What happens when the accomplishments that consumed my attention cannot accompany me into eternity?
Most importantly...
Am I in Christ?
Not merely, “Do I believe there is a God?”
Not, “Was I raised Christian?”
Not, “Do I sometimes attend church?”
Not, “Am I basically a decent person?”
Paul's hope is explicitly centered “ἐν τῷ Χριστῷ — en tō Christō” — in Christ.
This is where grief becomes more than grief.
It becomes a confrontation with eternity.
The Gospel tells us something our pride desperately resists hearing: our deepest problem is not simply that someday we will die.
Our deepest problem is sin.
Paul eventually brings us directly there:
“τὸ δὲ κέντρον τοῦ θανάτου ἡ ἁμαρτία...”
“The sting of death is sin.”
Sin is not merely a collection of embarrassing mistakes.
Sin is rebellion against the holy God who gave us life.
Every secret compromise.
Every carefully hidden appetite.
Every bitterness we have nurtured.
Every lie.
Every act of lust.
Every moment of pride.
Every idol.
Every time we wanted God’s gifts while resisting God Himself.
We have sinned.
And the Gospel does not rescue us by lowering God's holiness until our rebellion looks harmless.
God does something infinitely more costly.
He sends His Son.
Jesus enters the human story.
The sinless One walks among sinners.
The Holy One touches the unclean.
The rejected find Him.
The ashamed find Him.
The religiously impressive discover that they need Him just as desperately as everyone else.
Then Christ goes to the cross.
There, the scandal becomes almost unbearable.
The innocent One is condemned.
The righteous One is mocked.
The Creator is surrounded by His creatures.
Nails.
Blood.
Darkness.
A crown designed as mockery.
A cross designed as humiliation.
And Jesus dies.
Christianity never asks grieving people to worship a God unfamiliar with graves.
Jesus stood before the tomb of Lazarus and wept.
Jesus knows what human tears feel like.
And then Jesus Himself entered death.
But death encountered Someone it could not keep.
The tomb was sealed.
Then came the third day.
And the story changed forever.
This is why Paul's words later in 1 Corinthians 15 sound almost defiant:
“Κατεπόθη ὁ θάνατος εἰς νῖκος.”
“Death has been swallowed up in victory.”
Not ignored.
Not renamed.
Not romanticized.
Swallowed up.
Then Paul speaks directly to death:
“ποῦ σου, θάνατε, τὸ νῖκος; ποῦ σου, θάνατε, τὸ κέντρον;”
“Where, O death, is your victory? Where, O death, is your sting?”
Imagine saying those words beside a grave.
Not because graves do not hurt.
Not because Christians do not cry.
Not because separation suddenly becomes painless.
But because Jesus walked into death and came out alive.
The Christian does not stand beside a grave saying, “Death isn't real.”
The Christian stands there saying:
Death is real—but Jesus Christ is greater.
That is resurrection hope.
And it is radically different from vague spirituality.
Our hope is not merely that “people live on in our memories.”
Memories are precious.
But memories cannot resurrect anybody.
Our hope is not merely that someone is “watching over us.”
Our hope rests on something far more solid.
Jesus Christ has risen.
And those who belong to Him will be raised.
Paul says:
“τῷ δὲ θεῷ χάρις τῷ διδόντι ἡμῖν τὸ νῖκος διὰ τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ.”
“Thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.”
Notice where victory comes from.
Not through positive thinking.
Not through human goodness.
Not through religious achievement.
Through our Lord Jesus Christ.
That is the Gospel.
We do not climb our way toward God.
Christ came down for us.
We do not erase our own guilt.
Christ bore sin at the cross.
We do not defeat death.
Christ defeated it.
We do not earn resurrection.
Christ becomes our hope.
Grace does what we could never do for ourselves.
And perhaps somebody reading this has been avoiding Jesus because you think you have gone too far.
You know what you have done.
Other people may not.
God does.
You remember the night.
The betrayal.
The addiction.
The secret.
The person you hurt.
The years you wasted.
The prayers you stopped praying.
Maybe grief itself changed you.
You became angry with God.
You stopped going to church.
You could not understand why He allowed someone you loved to die.
Maybe you sat at the funeral surrounded by Christians singing about God's goodness while something inside you screamed:
Then why did He let this happen?
God is not frightened by that question.
The Bible contains grieving saints asking agonizing questions.
Faith does not mean pretending pain is painless.
But grief can become dangerous when pain persuades us to run from the only One who can ultimately redeem what death has stolen.
Jesus never promised His followers immunity from funerals.
He promised something greater.
Resurrection.
And resurrection means death does not get the last word over those who are Christ's.
Your tears matter.
Your grief matters.
That empty chair matters.
The person you lost mattered.
But hear this carefully:
Christian hope does not mean we can confidently declare the eternal destiny of every person simply because we loved them.
Scripture does not give us permission to manufacture assurance where God has not spoken.
Our hope is Christ.
And therefore grief also whispers an urgent question to the living:
What will you do with Jesus?
You are still breathing.
Your chair is occupied today.
Your heart is still beating.
Grace is being proclaimed to you right now.
Do not spend your entire life preparing for everything except eternity.
You can prepare for retirement and remain unprepared to meet God.
You can insure your house, insure your vehicle, protect your accounts, schedule medical examinations, build an inheritance, organize your funeral...
and never reconcile with the God before whom you will stand.
Jesus Christ calls sinners to repent and believe the Gospel.
Repentance is not paying God back.
You cannot.
It is turning from sin toward the Savior.
It is surrender.
It is finally admitting:
“Jesus, I cannot save myself.”
And perhaps the empty chair has made you realize something you were too busy to see.
Life is short.
Eternity is not.
Maybe there is someone you need to forgive.
Someone you need to call.
Someone who needs to hear, “I love you.”
Maybe there is a sin you need to stop protecting.
Maybe you have been performing Christianity while privately starving.
Maybe everyone around you thinks your faith is strong, but God knows you have been slowly drifting.
Come home.
Not to religion.
To Christ.
Come with the questions.
Come with the anger.
Come with the grief.
Come with the shame.
Come with trembling hands if necessary.
But come.
The cross tells you sin is more serious than you imagined.
The resurrection tells you Jesus is more powerful than you imagined.
And grace tells you your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
That is the heartbeat of everything we proclaim at Gospel Warrior:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
He rewrites sinners into sons and daughters.
He rewrites condemnation through forgiveness.
He rewrites rebellion through repentance.
He rewrites shame through grace.
And ultimately, for everyone who belongs to Him, He will rewrite even the grave through resurrection.
Maybe tonight your family will gather around a table with an empty chair.
Maybe Christmas hurts now.
Maybe birthdays hurt.
Maybe Sunday lunch feels different.
Maybe there are recipes you cannot cook without crying.
Let yourself miss them.
Love leaves an ache when someone is gone.
You do not dishonor Christ by grieving.
But do not let grief convince you that death is sovereign.
It isn't.
Jesus is.
One day Christ will demonstrate completely what Easter morning announced decisively.
Death's reign has been broken.
So cry.
Remember.
Grieve.
Tell the stories.
Hold the photographs.
Thank God for every mercy you were given.
But when the empty chair starts preaching despair, preach the resurrection back to it.
Christ has risen.
When the cemetery tells you death is undefeated:
Christ has risen.
When grief whispers that everything beautiful eventually disappears:
Christ has risen.
When your own mortality frightens you:
Christ has risen.
When Satan reminds you of forgiven sins:
Christ has risen.
When the darkness feels final:
Christ has risen.
And because Christ has risen, everyone who truly belongs to Him possesses a hope stronger than the grave.
Sometimes the most courageous sentence a grieving believer can write is simply:
Let other believers pray with you.
Your testimony may become the sentence another grieving person desperately needed tonight.
And if this confronted you about your own eternity, do not hide behind religious language.
“Jesus, I need You.”
Not because typing words saves anyone.
Christ saves.
But sometimes publicly admitting our need is the first crack in years of hiding.
Not fifty.
One.
The widow whose house became painfully quiet.
The father who buried a child.
The daughter who still reaches for her phone to call her mother.
The friend who stopped attending church after the funeral.
The believer smiling publicly while privately wondering whether God still sees them.
Not merely because an article deserves reach.
Your share may place resurrection hope in front of them at exactly the moment grief comes knocking.
Grief has seasons.
There may come another birthday, another anniversary, another ordinary Tuesday when you need to remember:
the grave is not greater than Jesus.
Supporting Gospel-centered work is not a substitute for supporting your local church, caring for your family, serving people in need, or giving as God leads you. Grace cannot be bought.
Share because somebody is grieving.
Tag because somebody is drifting.
Save because grief sometimes returns without warning.
And support the mission if God has genuinely placed that desire on your heart.
Because somewhere tonight there is an empty chair.
Someone will look at it.
Someone will remember.
Someone will cry after everyone else goes to sleep.
And someone desperately needs to know that Christianity does not answer that chair with a cliché.
It answers with an empty tomb.
The chair may remain empty in this present life.
The photographs may grow older while the face inside them never does.
The ache may remain in ways nobody else completely understands.
But for those who are in Jesus Christ, death does not possess the authority to write the ending.
Jesus does.
And perhaps that is the sentence you need to carry with you tonight:
The chair may be empty, but because the tomb of Jesus is empty, death will never have the final word over those who belong to Christ.
